Who is tracking us online and why?

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Your digital footprint is being tracked continuously. Have you become a willing victim of online stalking by corporates, criminals and governments?

Unique Selling Point:
Every single day we go online we leave a digital footprint. These footprints make us vulnerable to millions of people that might harm us. The advances and conveniences that technology brings, also force us to trade off some of our liberties and privacy.

Summary:
Not all tracking is bad but it does have it's negatives; governments monitor data in order to protect us, or in non-democratic states sensor and monitor descent. They may want to find out where a terrorist cell is going to strike, but they may also want to silence detractors, for example, in North Korea. We are also tracked by corporates and data aggregators that use market intelligence to target us with audience specific ads. Criminals pursue us to steal our identity and commit crimes by hacking into any connected device, using malware such as Trojans, RATS, Key Loggers and alike. Cracks and Hacks for Games and software often come with additional payloads to make money.

A look at the digital tracking industry reveals frightening and troubling trends, this is an opaque industry. Our online activity data is collected and aggregated into profiles that are sold on to third parties who will know who we are, where we are, what we are interested in and most likely predict what we will do in the future based on our past activities, all this without you knowing. Carte Blanche explores who is tracking who on line and why.

Further information:
We know that Google, Facebook, and Twitter collectively own more data about us than any other single entity in the world. What does this mean for individual users, and for society at large? Governments have a responsibility to protect us. Right now, aside from individual countries’ privacy laws, which were often created in the pre-internet era and apply only to what they call “personally identifiable information”, our right to privacy ends at these companies’ privacy policies, their terms of service, and their “I Accept Cookies” pop-ups. If we click to “accept”, then we compromise our privacy.

Commercial online tracking methodologies include, your GPS for example, which tracks you and others to help route you around traffic. Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, Google and many others use tracking to better target adverts to pay for the hundreds of millions in costs it takes to host everyone’s favorite online addictions. Criminals and governments also track online behavior and location, some for good and some for bad. Any device connected to a network is traceable, from location, to behavior, to the content and communications we send.

Some track us passively, some more aggressively, some do so with our consent and others such as criminals hack our systems to do so. This stems from our unwillingness to pay for the things we want and demand, trading off our privacy for free content and services. This information trade-off can be used for our protection, some for profit, and some for evil.

We unpack who is monitoring you and why. We will also talk with cyber sleuths on how you can increase your online security and protect your privacy and those around you.

We now live in a converged and connected world. Daily, more mobile devices get connected into the network and increase the chance of phishing criminals cracking in to our identity and committing more fraud. South Africans are not immune to this global problem.

Respected forensic investigator and internet sleuth Stieller Van Eeden exposes how the underworld operates online, and how they can target and track us. Stieler lurks within the web and catches some of the most brazen and intelligent cyber thieves. Our online behaviour and carelessness can put our lives, property and the lives of others at risk. He gives us tips on how we can up our defences so that we become less vulnerable.

Dino Kotsovos, will demonstrate how easy it is to track and exploit our online and mobile device weaknesses, based on our digital footprint and the kind of access we allow others.

We chat to Craig Mcleod, a seasoned IT expert and venture capitalist, he is a startups guru who worked for several notable successes including Thawte, which sold for $580 million. Craig will help us understand how the government monitors us and why we do not necessarily have to be overly paranoid about it, but others may disagree. The threat of security and terrorism is always at the forefront and that is the main reason why governments monitor their citizens. He gives us insight into the “other web” which intercepts all internet traffic, and is then shared amongst the '5 Eyes' alliance.

On the commercial side, Craig will show the digital trail we leave in our daily transactions. He takes us through an ordinary individual’s timeline on Google and how it is possible to see your every move if you have your location turned on. Many people are unaware that this function is happening in the background of their phones or their computers. He will also unpack how big business like Facebook, Google and Yahoo collects and tracks all our correspondence and why. Often it is our unwillingness to pay for stuff which leads us to volunteer our personal details that in turn allows companies to monitor us.

Craig gives a few simple steps on how we can improve our online privacy and understand more about online tracking, from basic browsing protection to cleaning your cookies to adding plugins that block third-party trackers.

A representative from Facebook Nunu Ntshingila, talks about the science behind commercial digital monitoring and tracking? There is great good that comes from market intelligence that is driven by data and science, many improvements to daily products and services enables businesses to reach a bigger testing sample and out of this great insight help shape brands. (NOT SURE I WILL GET THIS)

Imraan Kharwa of Smart Legal, is a privacy law expert who has researched the subject of online privacy for years, and on what we can do to safeguard our privacy and what rights we really do have. How does our country's law protect or compromise us? We will also find out if there is any recourse should our privacy be breached.

In conclusion, though some of the information is frightening, we “agree” that there are “trade-offs” we pay for progress, access and services, however there are steps we can take to improve our online security and be aware of what and where our digital footprint is going. We can also take measures through awareness that we don't have to “over share” our personal information.

Into the foreseeable future, tracking is here to stay so we need to ensure that we are safe and aware of our rights as well as our behaviour in cyberspace and that we do not give so much power away that malintentioned governments and organisations are able to take away our civil liberties and rights.

Press Release:


Who is Tracking You Online?
Are your net-surfing habits exposing your every move, from your shopping choices to travel arrangements and even your location? Every time we go online we leave a digital footprint, making us vulnerable to anyone from corporate marketing sleuths to criminals with malicious intent and even governments interested in our lives. Carte Blanche discovers how easy it is to exploit connected devices and track users’ online behaviour.

VO: So, if you've been hacked you've most likely been tracked. Be aware of the permissions you grant an app.

Carte Blanche brought together some of South Africa's foremost Cyber geeks and sleuths as they know full well how our digital footprint is being tracked continuously, by corporates, criminals and governments


VO: Meet ...Cyber sleuth Stieler Van Eeden



Stieler: Things are getting tight and criminals, are looking for various ways to target people.


VO: Legal Eagle in privacy Law Imraan Kharwa


Imraan: There is no shelf life to the things we put online, remember that we are free to chose but not free from the consequences of our choices


VO: Ethical Hacker extraordinaire Rob Len


ROB: Another issue is password reuse. Chances are, once I have your email address and your password, you've used the same one.


VO: Cyber security Analyst Simphiwe Mayisela


Simphiwe: If you want to attack an individual, any target commonly the first is tracking phase.


VO: Cyber Venture Capitalist and Entrepreneur Craig Mcleod

VO: Cyber Security Specialist - Dino Covotsos


Dino: We have our own monitoring in SA and it is believed that that monitoring is linked to the systems worldwide


VO: Internationally Russia's alleged hack of the US election goes to show that not only can you track people - you can influence large groups of people to do things, by creating and controlling information that is distributed. Every time we connect to the internet to react or contribute we leave a digital footprint which is cemented in cyberspace.


Craig: Something says here iam, this is what i'm saying at this exact moment in time. And from that we can get a whole lot about you.


VO: Commercial online tracking methodologies include, your GPS which tracks your physical location. Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, Google and many others use tracking to target adverts, which pay the costs of hosting everyone’s favourite online addictions.





Simphiwe: If you are not paying for a service you are the product and not the customer. If you look at Facebook, Facebook uses that information to build online interest based ads.



VO: These ads are based on the kind of websites you visit and are not necessarily targeted at you, but a group of people who have similar interests. On the other hand, hosts of webmail servers can monitor and gauge your interests through your daily communication.


Craig: If you look at your gmail a lot Iof what your mail content has been over the last four to six months has also very much driven what you're starting to notice in terms of banners.


VO: Rhet and Richard show us how we can check who our information is being shared with, using a clever tool like Ghostery


Richard: It's just a plug in on your web browser....
and that will show you all the trackers on the site and you can view and block them

Rhet: You have twenty four companies all keeping an eye on you, to see what they can sell you.


VO: Social media apps also collect message data which may be shared with 3rd parties. And then of course we are tracked in physical space with facilities like google maps, If we leave our location turned on on our phones.


Rhet: We can see he went on that day, from the store to a school, this information is stored constantly all the time.


VO: The protection of personal information Act or POPI, contains legislation which includes a prison sentence, of up to 10 years and up to 10 million rands penalties for non compliant businesses, for misuse of personal information.


Imraan: I'ts a very fine balancing act between publishing our personal information and obviously the protection that we have in terms of our law.


Bongani: Ja because Rob most of us think, I'm not that important, who wants my information? So I don't mind giving it out.

Rob: Just giving away information, checking in every time you go to the gym, where you have your coffee. I know your schedule.

Bongani: So who might YOU BE?
Rob: I could be a criminal, a stalker, someone with intent to do harm.


LINK:
Organised crime is big business, there are criminals lurking behind every unfortified network and once profiles and identities have been hijacked, untold damage can be caused. This is worth four hundred billion dollars every year.


Stieler: What we have to realise is that organisations have to protect thousands of users. And if I'm a cyber criminal I only need to infect one person in that organisation.





Bongani: How could I as I sit here, be a weak link?

Stieler: if you use a phone and you don't take ownership of that phone, there are various ways in which you become vulnerable.


Dino: I think just a bit of awareness on how to actually do certain things, like connect a VPN on your phone, a Virtual Private Network, will go a long way.


LINK:
For governments it's about law enforcement. They need to monitor everyone, particularly those that use online platforms to recruit and disseminate for criminal activity.


Dino: Evidence is substantial that we are being monitored 24/7, so everything are easily available for governments to actually get into your phone and take a look at any point in time.


Craig: There are the systems they are allowed to listen to, and of course the systems they are not allowed, and there is not a big distinction between the two.


VO: Digital communication is monitored throughout the world, most prominently by the so called ECHELON surveillance system operated by the Five Eyes Intelligence pact. It is a common activity for Governments to shop around for malware or software to enable them to monitor people more effectively.


Imraan: The only justification government needs to monitor you is that there may be the commission of a crime or there is the suspicion of the commission a crime.


Craig: There is also an argument to say that this is to prevent terrorists and if we start preventing that, if we start telling the bad guys how we're monitoring them and they move to other means, we're going to start missing more and more of these crimes.


VO: Digital tracking is here to stay, but the advances and convenience that technology brings, also force us to trade off some of our liberties and privacy. This was prophesied as early as the 1930's.


Imraan: Aldous Huxley said we will not be forced to give up our freedoms, but instead we will be so inundated with pleasures that we will gladly give them up.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Your digital footprint is being tracked continuously. Have you become a willing victim of online stalking by corporates, criminals and governments?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Every single day we go online we leave a digital footprint. These footprints make us vulnerable to millions of people that might harm us. The advances and conveniences that technology brings, also force us to trade off some of our liberties and privacy.
metadata.Summary: Not all tracking is bad but it does have it's negatives; governments monitor data in order to protect us, or in non-democratic states sensor and monitor descent. They may want to find out where a terrorist cell is going to strike, but they may also want to silence detractors, for example, in North Korea. We are also tracked by corporates and data aggregators that use market intelligence to target us with audience specific ads. Criminals pursue us to steal our identity and commit crimes by hacking into any connected device, using malware such as Trojans, RATS, Key Loggers and alike. Cracks and Hacks for Games and software often come with additional payloads to make money. A look at the digital tracking industry reveals frightening and troubling trends, this is an opaque industry. Our online activity data is collected and aggregated into profiles that are sold on to third parties who will know who we are, where we are, what we are interested in and most likely predict what we will do in the future based on our past activities, all this without you knowing. Carte Blanche explores who is tracking who on line and why.
metadata.Further information: We know that Google, Facebook, and Twitter collectively own more data about us than any other single entity in the world. What does this mean for individual users, and for society at large? Governments have a responsibility to protect us. Right now, aside from individual countries’ privacy laws, which were often created in the pre-internet era and apply only to what they call “personally identifiable information”, our right to privacy ends at these companies’ privacy policies, their terms of service, and their “I Accept Cookies” pop-ups. If we click to “accept”, then we compromise our privacy. Commercial online tracking methodologies include, your GPS for example, which tracks you and others to help route you around traffic. Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, Google and many others use tracking to better target adverts to pay for the hundreds of millions in costs it takes to host everyone’s favorite online addictions. Criminals and governments also track online behavior and location, some for good and some for bad. Any device connected to a network is traceable, from location, to behavior, to the content and communications we send. Some track us passively, some more aggressively, some do so with our consent and others such as criminals hack our systems to do so. This stems from our unwillingness to pay for the things we want and demand, trading off our privacy for free content and services. This information trade-off can be used for our protection, some for profit, and some for evil. We unpack who is monitoring you and why. We will also talk with cyber sleuths on how you can increase your online security and protect your privacy and those around you. We now live in a converged and connected world. Daily, more mobile devices get connected into the network and increase the chance of phishing criminals cracking in to our identity and committing more fraud. South Africans are not immune to this global problem. Respected forensic investigator and internet sleuth Stieller Van Eeden exposes how the underworld operates online, and how they can target and track us. Stieler lurks within the web and catches some of the most brazen and intelligent cyber thieves. Our online behaviour and carelessness can put our lives, property and the lives of others at risk. He gives us tips on how we can up our defences so that we become less vulnerable. Dino Kotsovos, will demonstrate how easy it is to track and exploit our online and mobile device weaknesses, based on our digital footprint and the kind of access we allow others. We chat to Craig Mcleod, a seasoned IT expert and venture capitalist, he is a startups guru who worked for several notable successes including Thawte, which sold for $580 million. Craig will help us understand how the government monitors us and why we do not necessarily have to be overly paranoid about it, but others may disagree. The threat of security and terrorism is always at the forefront and that is the main reason why governments monitor their citizens. He gives us insight into the “other web” which intercepts all internet traffic, and is then shared amongst the '5 Eyes' alliance. On the commercial side, Craig will show the digital trail we leave in our daily transactions. He takes us through an ordinary individual’s timeline on Google and how it is possible to see your every move if you have your location turned on. Many people are unaware that this function is happening in the background of their phones or their computers. He will also unpack how big business like Facebook, Google and Yahoo collects and tracks all our correspondence and why. Often it is our unwillingness to pay for stuff which leads us to volunteer our personal details that in turn allows companies to monitor us. Craig gives a few simple steps on how we can improve our online privacy and understand more about online tracking, from basic browsing protection to cleaning your cookies to adding plugins that block third-party trackers. A representative from Facebook Nunu Ntshingila, talks about the science behind commercial digital monitoring and tracking? There is great good that comes from market intelligence that is driven by data and science, many improvements to daily products and services enables businesses to reach a bigger testing sample and out of this great insight help shape brands. (NOT SURE I WILL GET THIS) Imraan Kharwa of Smart Legal, is a privacy law expert who has researched the subject of online privacy for years, and on what we can do to safeguard our privacy and what rights we really do have. How does our country's law protect or compromise us? We will also find out if there is any recourse should our privacy be breached. In conclusion, though some of the information is frightening, we “agree” that there are “trade-offs” we pay for progress, access and services, however there are steps we can take to improve our online security and be aware of what and where our digital footprint is going. We can also take measures through awareness that we don't have to “over share” our personal information. Into the foreseeable future, tracking is here to stay so we need to ensure that we are safe and aware of our rights as well as our behaviour in cyberspace and that we do not give so much power away that malintentioned governments and organisations are able to take away our civil liberties and rights.
